claims.claim: The Sun's tide-generating force is about half the Moon's (NOAA: 'about half'; NASA: 'a little less than half'): the Sun has about 27 million times the Moon's mass but is about 390 times farther away.
claims.note: Two independent agency pages, both read. Say 'about half' or 'a little less than half'; the precise 46% seen in a weather-site snippet is not used.

claims.claim: Spring tides come at full and new Moon, when Earth, Sun and Moon line up; neap tides come around the first and last quarter, when Sun and Moon are at right angles.
claims.note: Read in NASA's page; NOAA's variations page agrees but was seen only as a snippet. Textbook astronomy, so low risk.

claims.claim: Because the Moon moves along its orbit, a point on Earth needs about 50 minutes more than a day to turn back under it (NASA: 'The extra time is ~50 mins').
claims.note: The film's 'high water at about the same hour every day' without the Moon is reasoned from this (subject M6), not a sourced claim.

claims.claim: Hundreds of species of corals and other invertebrates spawn at the same time several nights after the full Moon (the Great Barrier Reef mass spawning; Harrison et al. 1984 as cited by the review).
claims.note: Read in the review; the primary study is known only through it. Say 'several nights after the full Moon', not a fixed night.

claims.claim: Colonies of the brooding coral Pocillopora damicornis kept under constant full-moon or constant new-moon conditions released their larvae out of synchrony (Jokiel et al. 1985 as cited by the review).
claims.note: One experiment on one species, and larval release in a brooding coral, not reef mass spawning. The narration must say 'one coral, in one experiment' and never extend it to every reef. If this stays the key moment, read Jokiel et al. 1985 before the script.

claims.claim: In corals the light-sensing gene cry2 was expressed more on full-moon nights than on new-moon nights, which the review says suggests a key role in timing spawning (Levy et al., as cited by the review).
claims.note: The role is the review's 'suggesting'; keep that hedge. Not carried by the chosen film (see notes.md).

claims.claim: In the marine midge Clunio marinus, moonlight sets the monthly (semilunar) timing in southern populations, while northern populations use water turbulence instead (Neumann 1975, 1988 as cited by the review).
claims.note: Whether the northern cue is the tides' own churn, which would make even the backup clock the Moon's, was not checked. Do not say it until Neumann's work is read.

claims.claim: Night animals behave differently with moonlight: eagle owls call more often, from higher perches, on moonlit nights (Penteriani et al. 2011); coyotes howl to hold territory more often on new-moon nights (Bender et al. 1996); migrating land birds set off more often as moonlight decreases (Pyle et al. 1993); all as cited by the review.
claims.note: Each rests on one study, read through the review. Left out on purpose: the review's lions attacking people and blood-feeding bats (content rules).

claims.claim: How animals sense and respond to lunar time is still poorly understood: the review says the mechanisms are 'even less understood' and lists as open questions whether animals carry internal lunar-day or lunar-month clocks.
claims.note: Grounds the speculative value R5: the film says nobody knows how moon-timed life would cope.

claims.claim: Geological records give an Earth spinning about 1.22 times faster than today 2.5 billion years ago, slowed since by tidal dissipation (Laskar et al. 1993, citing Williams 1990).
claims.note: The geological record itself (Williams 1990) was not read. Spinning 1.22 times faster means a day of about 24 / 1.22 = 19.7 hours, 'about 20 hours': arithmetic, not a separate claim.

claims.claim: Today the Moon keeps Earth's tilt (obliquity) stable; without the Moon the tilt would vary chaotically.
claims.note: Two independent primary studies read: Laskar et al. 1993 in full, Li & Batygin 2014 as an abstract. How far and how fast the tilt would go is C13 and C14, not this claim.

claims.claim: With the Moon, Earth's tilt varies only about 1.3 degrees either side of a mean of 23.3 degrees (Laskar et al. 1993).
claims.note: One primary source; the figure is the paper's own.

claims.claim: With the Moon removed and Earth's present parameters kept, an earlier calculation reported in Laskar et al. (1993) gave tilt variations from 15 to 32 degrees within 1 million years.
claims.note: This is the case closest to the premise (today's Earth, Moon removed). The paper's famous 0-85 degree range is for faster spins (1.22 and 1.6 times today's) and the long term. A 2004 abstract (S7, snippet only) is said to give 12-38 degrees over 100 million years: a lead that roughly agrees. Always say it as 'one calculation'.

claims.claim: How far and how fast a moonless Earth's tilt would wander in the long run is disputed. Laskar et al. (1993) find chaotic swings reaching more than 50 degrees within a few million years and more than 85 degrees in the long term, for many primordial spin rates (their detailed runs use 1.22 and 1.6 times today's spin). Li & Batygin (2014) find the chaotic change slow enough not to rule out long-term habitability. Lissauer et al. (2012) are reported to find a much narrower range over billions of years.
claims.note: Both sides read in primary form (S4 in full, S5 as an abstract); S6 seen only in search summaries, so its 'narrower range' is not said until read. Present it as an open scientific disagreement and give each figure with its study and conditions.

claims.claim: Milankovitch theory links the ice ages to changes in sunlight at northern latitudes caused by changes in Earth's orbit and orientation (precession, eccentricity and obliquity).
claims.note: As stated in the opening sentence of Laskar et al. 1993; Milankovitch's own work was not read.

claims.claim: Without the Moon, Earth could go from almost no tilt to a drastic tilt, with extreme seasons and ice ages, in just a few hundred thousand years.
claims.note: A popular claim, seen only in a search summary of a magazine piece. For today's Earth it goes beyond the studies read: Laskar et al.'s own calculation for today's spin gives 15-32 degrees within a million years, and later work finds the drift slow. Popular figures also disagree with each other (S10: 10-45 degrees). Not to be used; recorded so the script stage does not pick it up.

claims.claim: Laskar et al. (1993) state that, with the Moon, the tilt stays nearly fixed, with only small swings, until tidal dissipation in the end drives Earth into the large chaotic zone.
claims.note: Supports only the alternative T4. The paper gives no date for it.
